name: Sam Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Sam. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and what you say here is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm self-employed, a contractor for one of the parcel networks, and I cover the whole Ashdale valley in my own van. That's about 110 drops spread over 70 miles of single-track roads. I'm the senior driver for the valley, so when someone's off I take their bit too, and I train the cover drivers on the farm tracks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people know me, I know which barn to leave stuff in and which granny wants it on the chair by the door. What wears me out is the van, it's a 2016 Transit on finance at £290 a month, and the network docks me if I miss a slot. Friday and Saturday nights I do takeaway runs from the Golden Dragon in town on the food app to keep up with the payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss for nothing much. Most folk round here would say the same. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not on that stuff much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't change my problem, which is the van and the money. The network cut what they pay per parcel twice in three years. I've got maybe three weeks of money if the van's off the road, and then I'm stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now: the valley route, weekend takeaway, and keep the van going. I'd do the servicing myself where I can, to save the garage bill. And I'd keep an eye out in case the bus company or the quarry wanted drivers, though that rarely happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. A bit tense under the surface, like waiting for the next bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the van fails its test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm borrowing from my dad or putting it on a card, and I can't work till it's fixed. Last time it was a clutch and I lost four days. Hannah, my girlfriend, works mornings at the bakery, but that only just covers her half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI or new tech in your work at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just the scanner and the route app the network makes us use, and I ignore the route order half the time because it doesn't know the valley. I don't use those chatbot things. Never seen the point.

say: All that fuss for **nothing much**, most folk round here would say.
I wouldn't post anything, I'm **not online** much.
think: My problem is still **the van** and the money, AI or not.
The network has cut **pay per parcel** twice in three years.
do: Keep the **valley route** and weekend takeaway runs.
Do **van servicing** myself to save garage bills.
Watch for **driving jobs** at the bus company or quarry.
feel: **Tense** under the surface, like waiting for the next bill.
S0.quote: I ignore the route order half the time because the app doesn't know the valley.
fieldNote: His worry is the **£290 van finance**, not technology.
He trusts his **local knowledge** over the network's route app.
Few jobs nearby means his backup is just **hoping** for a quarry or bus opening.

steps.text: Keep the Ashdale valley route and weekend takeaway runs
Service the Transit himself instead of paying the garage
Ask the quarry and bus company about driver openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office types who need to worry, not drivers. Somebody's still got to get a parcel up a farm track. I'd say that at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the network would use AI to plan routes and set pay even tighter. That's my rate going down again, probably, and more checks on my times. The driving itself, up here, I can't see a robot doing it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and not go chasing new things. I'd try to get the network to keep me on the valley, because I'm the only one who knows it. Maybe I'd ask Hannah if we could cut the takeaway nights and sell the second car we barely use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like the rates are going to get squeezed again and I can't stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't chase new things. What if the network said you had to use a new AI app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it, because I'd have to, but I wouldn't like it. I'd still drive the valley my way. The app can sulk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your rate dropped again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, it's an old Fiesta that sits outside most of the week. Then going out on Saturdays, which we barely do anyway. After that there's not much left to cut.

say: It's the **office types** who need to worry, not drivers.
Somebody still has to get a parcel up a **farm track**.
think: The network would use AI to set **pay** even tighter.
Robots won't manage the **valley roads** for years.
do: Keep going as now and **avoid** chasing new things.
Ask the network to keep him on the **valley route**.
Sell the **old Fiesta** if rates drop again.
feel: **Uneasy**, sensing another squeeze he can't stop.
S1.quote: Somebody's still got to get a parcel up a farm track.
fieldNote: He expects AI to show up as **lower rates**, not lost driving.
He would use a new app only **under protest**.
Cuts are already near the bone: after the **second car**, little is left.

steps.text: Ask the network to keep him on the valley route
Sell the old Fiesta that sits outside most of the week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone in government had better have a plan, because two years is nothing. People round here would be angry. I'd probably say less and listen more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, thinking AI in 2028 doesn't drive my van, but robots by 2031 might, at least on the main road. The valley tracks maybe later. I'd be about 32 with a van on finance and no other skills, and that frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to pay off the van early, so if the work goes I at least own something I could sell or use. I'd look harder for the quarry or a farm job, something with my hands. And I'd talk to my dad about working on his mate's farm if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but trying not to show it to Hannah.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hide it from Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because she'd worry more than me, and she's already worried about her hours at the bakery. I'd tell her once I had a plan. That's how my dad did things, for better or worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a farm job safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever, if robots are as good as people. But farms round here are small and old, and nobody's buying a robot for forty sheep. It'd buy me time, I think.

say: Someone in **government** had better have a plan, because two years is nothing.
think: Robots by **2031** could take the main road route first, the tracks later.
At 32 I'd have **van finance** and no other skills.
do: Pay off the **van** early so I own something.
Look harder for a **quarry or farm** job.
Ask Dad about work on his **mate's farm**.
feel: **Scared**, but hiding it from his girlfriend Hannah.
S2.quote: Nobody's buying a robot for forty sheep.
fieldNote: He knows **robots by 2031** reach his valley eventually, starting with the main road.
He **hides** fear from his partner until he has a plan, as his father did.
His fallbacks are **family contacts** and small farms, not courses.

steps.text: Pay extra each month to clear the van finance early
Apply for labouring work at the quarry
Ask his dad about work on his friend's sheep farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not panic, but the government should get on with it. That's what I'd say at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, with robots around 2034, I'd have a good few years of driving left. Long enough to clear the van and maybe save a bit. The valley might be one of the last places they reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the van finance in the next two years and then put that £290 a month aside. I'd keep the takeaway nights. If the quarry ever offered a loader licence course, I'd take it, because that's still driving, just different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it's not on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do any course at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it's paid and nearby, and only for something I can see the point of. A loader licence, yes. Sitting at a computer, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hannah say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd want me to do more, she always does. She'd say, Sam, you can't drive forever. She's probably right, but I'd still wait to see what happens first.

say: We've got **five years**, so no panic, but government should get moving.
I'd say that at the **pub**, not online.
think: Robots around **2034** leave a good few years of driving.
The **valley** might be one of the last places robots reach.
do: Clear the **van finance** within two years.
Save the freed **£290 a month** afterwards.
Take a **loader licence** course if the quarry offers one.
feel: **Uneasy**, aware of it but not crushed by it.
S3.quote: My girlfriend Hannah would say, Sam, you can't drive forever. She's probably right, but I'd still wait to see what happens first.
fieldNote: The extra years let him plan around **owning the van** outright.
He would only retrain for something **hands-on** and nearby.
He admits he would **wait and see**, against Hannah's advice.

steps.text: Clear the van finance within two years
Take a quarry loader licence course if one is offered
Wait to see what the network does before changing jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can happen. No point worrying people now. I'd say that to the other drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, robots in 2039 means I'd be 40, and I'd hope to have something else by then. But I know myself, I'd probably still be in the van. The money would still be tight either way, that's the real thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, own the van, and maybe in five years think about a farm or quarry job. I'd try to save something, even £50 a month. I'd keep the takeaway nights as long as the Golden Dragon is open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less worried about robots, still worried about money. That's normal for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably still be in the van. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd like to say I'd plan, but I don't really. My dad drove a milk lorry for 30 years and that was fine for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long warning change anything for you and Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd think about a house in the valley, a small one. If I knew I had ten years of driving, I could maybe get a mortgage. That's the only way it'd change things.

say: **Ten years** is a long time, and plenty can happen.
think: At 40 in **2039**, I'd probably still be in the van.
**Tight money** is the real thing, whatever robots do.
do: Own the van and **carry on** driving.
Look at **farm or quarry** work in about five years.
feel: **Less worried** about robots, still worried about money.
S4.quote: My dad drove a milk lorry for 30 years and that was fine for him.
fieldNote: He models his future on his **father's career**, which was steady.
Long warning opens one idea: a **small house** in the valley.
Thin savings keep him **anxious** even when robots are far off.

steps.text: Keep driving the valley route in his own van
Save fifty pounds a month toward a house deposit
Look into buying a small house in the valley with Hannah

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd still be paying for a van that robots would make useless. What would help is a fair price for my route if the network replaced me, and help finding real work nearby, not courses in a city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what happens to the people on the routes. My drivers know every old lady who can't get to the door. A robot leaves the parcel and goes. Somebody should think about that.

headlineQuote: My drivers know every old lady who can't get to the door. A robot leaves the parcel and goes.
portrait: Sam is 27, a **self-employed** parcel driver covering the rural Ashdale valley in a financed Transit.
He lives with **Hannah**, who works mornings at a bakery, and has about three weeks saved.
He is **pragmatic** and wary of tech, ignoring the route app when it doesn't know the valley.
He leans on **family and local work** rather than courses, and tends to wait and see.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving him paying off a van that robots make useless.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair payout** for his route if replaced.
Help finding **real local work**, not city courses.
